Ownership and Borrowing: Referee vs the Borrow Checker

Rust and SLA both guarantee memory safety, but their checking models are completely different: Rust uses the compile-time borrow checker plus the type system to distinguish read from write, while SLA hands this to SA's Referee bitmask verifier. This page compares the two models item by item, explains SLA's two design red lines (do not give up ^, do not introduce mut), and gives the phased plan for introducing mutability.

The Two Checking Models

DimensionRust borrow checkerSA Referee (behind SLA)
How read/write are distinguishedType system: &T read-only, &mut T exclusive writeOnly one syntax, &; dynamically determined from whether there is a store after the borrowed view as Locked_Read / Locked_Mut
Ownership transferImplicit move on assignment/argument passing^x prefix explicitly declares it (in most scenarios you can rely on automatic moves)
Resource releaseDrop traitCompiler implicitly injects !, not written on the user surface
Data race preventionSend/Sync compile-time solvingAffine mask + cross-core validation
Cross-function borrowing safetyGuaranteed at compile timeFrontend responsibility model (the FAQ explicitly acknowledges a lower-bound gap here)
Verifier sizeAbout 200K linesTarget ≤2500 lines, can be formally proven (Coq / FPGA programming is on the roadmap)

The checking cost gap is one source of SLA's compilation speed promise. By the target framing in the 2026-06-15 snapshot: borrow-checking 1000 functions takes Rust NLL about 1-3 seconds, and SLA about 10 milliseconds (O(1) bitmask, claimed 100-300×); these are design target values, not measured benchmark reports.

Three User-Surface Symbols in the Five-Symbol Contract

SA's ownership contract consists of five symbols: = & ^ ! *. The SLA user surface directly touches three of them:

Rust spellingSLA spellingDifference notes
&x / &mut x&xCreates a borrowed view, automatically unlocked at the end of scope; read/write are dynamically determined by the Referee, not distinguished at the syntax level
Implicit move (let b = a;)let b = ^a;SLA explicitly marks the transfer with the ^ prefix; method calls automatically borrow/automatically move according to the receiver signature
impl Drop / manual releaseNo counterpart! is implicitly injected by the compiler after live-variable analysis at branch merge points; it is not written in source code

A variable that has been moved is marked Consumed in the frontend, and using it again produces a clear UseAfterMove compile error — consistent with the SA Referee's interception semantics, except that the error is raised earlier, at the SLA layer.

Explicit Move vs Implicit Move

// Rust：转移发生在赋值的瞬间，源码上没有任何痕迹
let a = make_value();
let b = a;              // 隐式 move，a 从此不可用
// 再用 a → 编译错误
// Sla：转移是一个看得见的操作
let a = make_value();
let b = ^a;             // ^ 前缀 = Move
// 再用 a → UseAfterMove 编译错误

Method calls follow the same rules (UFCS static expansion): if the first parameter of the signature is &T it borrows automatically (v.len() → len(&v)), and if the first parameter is a value type it moves automatically (v.push(1) → push(^v, 1)).

Two Red Lines

The surface compatibility assessment drew two lines that must not be crossed in order to “make SLA more like Rust”:

Red lineCorresponding design principle
Do not give up ^The core physical input of the five-symbol contract + affine state machine; removing it collapses SA's verification model
Do not introduce mutShared read vs exclusive write is dynamically decided by the Referee in the runtime context, not distinguished at the syntax level; &mut is a redundant declaration here, and “one fewer prefix = a lower LLM error rate”

There is also a common worry about ^ — will it clash with Rust's XOR? The answer is no: SLA's ^x is a prefix unary operator, while Rust's a ^ b is an infix binary operator, and the two are in different parser contexts and can coexist (see the Syntax Comparison Matrix (Measured) page for the parsing rules).

Three Phases of Mutability

The core conclusion of the mutability decision (v0.2 finalized, 2026-06-15) is: let mut will never be introduced; &mut is introduced according to engineering trigger conditions, rather than immediately.

ItemPhase 1 (current)Phase 2 (before the sa3d ECS launch)
let x = 5 binding mutabilityMutable by default (unchanged)Mutable by default (unchanged)
const x = 5 bindingImmutable (unchanged)Immutable (unchanged)
let mut x = 5 spellingNot introducedNot introduced
&self in impl/traitCovers read and write (current convention)Read only; writes require &mut self
&mut T borrow typeNot introducedIntroduced
Trait method &mut selfNot introducedIntroduced (forced contract)
Impact on lowered SANoneZero impact (still degrades to SA &)
Impact on existing SLA codeZero changesWrite-method signatures change to &mut self, migrated automatically by tooling
Rust surface compatibilityAbout 70%About 85%

The Phase 1 convention has been validated by real demos: demos/rosetta/59_method_counter/main.sla uses fn inc(&self) containing an incrementing write operation, and demos/rosetta/40_impl_block_state/main.sla modifies state inside &self, and both work normally — the read/write distinction is borne by the SA Referee after lowering. The hard trigger for Phase 2 is that the ECS parallel scheduler needs static read/write sets: if move_sys writes Pos while render_sys reads Pos, the scheduler must know this to decide on serialization; if both are written as &Pos it can only conservatively serialize everything. A migration tool sa migrate sla-add-mut will be provided alongside to scan function bodies for write operations and automatically change signatures.

NoteIntroducing &mut in Phase 2 is not a philosophical turn — the Referee at SA's physical layer still dynamically determines read/write; introducing it only supplements static information for the ECS scheduler. Only in Phase 3 (when a library ecosystem has formed) will borrow errors be upgraded to precise errors at the SLA source level.

No memory leaks✅✅

Rust → SLA Migration Quick Reference

Rust spellingCurrent SLA equivalent
let mut x = 5;let x = 5;
fn inc(&mut self)fn inc(&self)
&mut x&x
impl Drop for TNo counterpart; cleanup is managed by the compiler
'a lifetime annotationsJust delete them (parsed but ignored)
WarningThe easiest pitfall when migrating from Rust is treating &T as read-only: under SLA's current convention it covers both read and write, and you cannot tell from the signature whether a method will change state. This gap of “signatures do not express mutability” will only close after Phase 2 introduces &mut self.

Key Points of This Page

  • Both sides give guarantees of no UAF/double-free/leaks/use-after-move; the difference is in the verification mechanism and verifier size.
  • SLA has only one borrowing syntax, with read/write dynamically determined by the Referee; this is the physical basis for the “do not introduce mut” red line.
  • ^ makes ownership transfer explicit and does not conflict with Rust's infix XOR.
  • let mut will never be introduced; &mut T/&mut self are Phase 2 engineering-trigger items.
  • Differences at the macro level often affect porting effort more than ownership does; see the Macros and Metaprogramming Compared page.
